Never, at least not from flow. The premise is a myth: glass is an amorphous solid, and at room temperature it doesn't flow on any timescale that matters. Calculations of the relaxation time for window glass run to many times the age of the universe, so your windows will be the same shape in a billion years as they are now.

Old panes are uneven because of how they were made. Crown glass was spun into discs, which left panes of varying thickness. Glaziers often installed the heavier edge down for stability, which is why you see "thicker at the bottom" in some church windows. But plenty of old panes are thicker at the top or the sides, which wouldn't happen if flow were the cause. Medieval glass that has survived in good condition and Roman glass vessels, still sharp-edged after 2,000 years, also show no sag.

Optical instruments tell the same story: old telescope lenses from the 1600s and 1700s retain their precise figures.
